title: Memory-Free Continual Learning with Null Space Adaptation for Zero-Shot Vision-Language Models
one_liner: NuSA-CL updates a vision-language model inside directions that disturb old behavior as little as possible, so it can learn new tasks without replay buffers or stored past data.
lead: Zero-shot vision-language models such as CLIP already know broad visual concepts from large pretraining. In deployment, they still need to adapt to new tasks, new classes, or new environments. Standard continual learning methods often store old examples or distill from old checkpoints to avoid catastrophic forgetting. Those tools add memory and computation costs. NuSA-CL takes a different route. It uses low-rank adaptation, which means it learns only a small update written as the product of two small tables of numbers, and restricts that update to an approximate null space of the current model. Null space here means directions where changes to the model weights cause little first-order change in the model's existing outputs. If updates stay in those directions, new learning interferes less with what the model already knows.

problem.h2: Why adapting a zero-shot model usually destroys old ability
paras: A vision-language model has many stored weights shared across tasks. When you fine-tune it on a new stream of data, the update that improves the new task usually changes those shared weights in directions that also matter for old tasks. The result is catastrophic forgetting: gains on the new task arrive by overwriting old decision boundaries and language-image associations.

Replay buffers reduce that problem by showing old examples again, and distillation reduces it by forcing the new model to mimic the old one. Both strategies are costly in a real deployment because they require storing past data, extra forward passes, or both. The question is whether the model can protect old behavior through the direction of the update itself rather than through external memory.

callout.html: Only adapt the model along weight directions that have minimal effect on its current outputs, so new learning uses spare degrees of freedom instead of rewriting the old ones.

steps.text: The method identifies weight directions where small movement changes the current model outputs very little.

steps.b: Write the update in low-rank form
steps.text: Only a small number of trainable factors are learned, which keeps the adaptation lightweight.

steps.b: Project the update into the null space
steps.text: The task-specific change is constrained to stay inside the low-interference subspace, so the update avoids directions that would strongly affect older behavior.

steps.b: Train on the current task without replay
steps.text: No old examples are stored or revisited; protection comes from the update direction itself.
Each new task gets its own constrained update while the shared pretrained backbone remains largely stable.

paras: The paper changes where adaptation is allowed to happen. Instead of updating arbitrary weight directions, it limits learning to a subspace chosen for low interference with the current model.

hidden.h2: Interference comes from update direction, not just update size
hidden.name: weight directions that preserve current behavior
paras: The hidden quantity is the set of weight directions that the current model can move along with little immediate effect on its present outputs. A large update in one of those directions may do less damage than a small update in a highly sensitive direction.

That matters because continual learning failure is not caused only by how much the model moves. It is caused by where it moves. NuSA-CL tries to spend adaptation in directions that are weakly coupled to old behavior, so the model can absorb new information without paying for it by erasing zero-shot transfer.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the directions and outcomes that control whether adaptation interferes with old knowledge.

reads.html: Some weight directions are dangerous because they quickly change old predictions, while others are comparatively safe. The method tries to update only in the safer set.
Continual adaptation is constrained to an approximate null space of the current model, so task learning proceeds in directions with minimal first-order effect on existing zero-shot behavior.

paras: To first order, a small parameter update changes the model output according to the Jacobian, which is the local sensitivity of outputs to parameters. If an update lies in a null-space direction of that sensitivity map, the immediate output change is near zero. That gives a principled definition of low interference.

NuSA-CL approximates those directions and then restricts a low-rank adapter to them. Low-rank means the update is written as the product of two small matrices, so only a compact number of trainable values is added. The projection step is the important part: the adapter may want to move in any direction to reduce the current task loss, but only the component inside the null space is kept. This works because the discarded component is the one most likely to alter current outputs strongly.

The reason this can replace replay or distillation is that the protection signal is built into the parameterization. Replay protects old tasks by showing them again. Distillation protects old tasks by matching old outputs explicitly. NuSA-CL protects them by making it hard for optimization to step into directions known to affect them. That does not make forgetting impossible, but it lowers interference enough to preserve much more zero-shot ability at low memory cost.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the raw task update has two parts: one safe component of size 3 and one harmful component of size 4.
The null-space basis captures only the safe component.
After projection, the harmful component is removed and the applied update has size 3 in the safe direction only.
The new task still improves if that safe component reduces its loss.
Old zero-shot behavior changes less because the omitted harmful component was the part most strongly tied to current outputs.

math.note: The method does not ask optimization to remember old data. It changes the update rule so only low-interference movement is possible.

bars.h2: Why the constraint is useful in practice

charts.title: Ordinary memory-free fine-tuning
charts.note: Memory use stays low, but forgetting is severe because the update can move through highly sensitive directions.

charts.title: NuSA-CL projected low-rank updates
charts.note: Retention improves because the update is confined to low-interference directions while keeping the lightweight low-rank form.

items.b: The null space is only approximate.
items.html: If the estimated low-interference directions are inaccurate, the projected update may still change old outputs substantially, because the true sensitivity structure was mismeasured.

items.b: Some new tasks need sensitive directions.
items.html: A task that conflicts strongly with the current model may require movement outside the allowed subspace. In that case, strict projection can protect old ability but cap new-task learning.

items.b: Repeated tasks can fill the spare subspace.
items.html: After many sequential tasks, the remaining low-interference capacity may shrink, so later tasks have less room to adapt without causing interference.

The method is strongest when new tasks are related enough to use residual degrees of freedom in the pretrained model, because then the null-space constraint blocks harmful rewriting without blocking all useful learning.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a pretrained CLIP-style model and train it on a short sequence of image classification tasks without replay data. Compare ordinary low-rank fine-tuning against null-space-projected low-rank fine-tuning. Measure both current-task accuracy and retained zero-shot accuracy on earlier tasks after each stage. The demo should also visualize how much of each raw update is removed by the projection.
demo.closing: The demo must show that the gain comes from changing update direction rather than merely shrinking update size.
